prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a clean mechanism-level achievement: the magic-wavelength condition removes the lattice light shift while confining many atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and this one idea is what lets a simple, general design reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. It is independently reproduced in many laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) and in several species, it opens tests of constants, relativistic redshift over millimetres and geodesy, and it underlies the coming redefinition of the second. Attribution is the cleanest on the list: Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for the record accuracy and the many-body clock physics. Seven of eight members place it in their top four, and after hearing the attribution arguments around my own first choice (KPZ) I am comfortable putting the clock first.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier clock-related prizes (Hall and Haensch 2005 for the comb, Wineland 2012 for ion control), and the view that this is an instrument advance rather than a discovery. A second concern is that Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others have real claims to parts of the history, so a two-name prize is a simplification. Finally, the pending SI redefinition could make a slightly later date arguably better timed, though I do not think waiting improves the scientific case.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as the cleanest new measurement method that changed what can be measured, and notes that earlier comb and trapping prizes keep this award focused.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and have moved toward it. My own opening placed KPZ first, but only I supported it, and the lack of a clean credit line is a real defect there. I would qualify one point: the prior prizes help focus the award only if the citation is worded around the magic-wavelength lattice and the resulting accuracy, not around clocks in general. Otherwise the comb and ion prizes make the committee's objection easy to state.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first but stresses that the committee must be convinced it is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and that the weight between Katori's proposal and Ye's later milestones is uncertain.
responses.response: I think the distinctness question is answerable: the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a frequency ruler, and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions, whereas the lattice clock is a different mechanism, many neutral atoms interrogated with the light shift cancelled. On the Katori/Ye weighting I would not rank them. Katori's proposal makes the device possible and Ye's work shows what it can do, and those are two decisive and complementary contributions. I would be more concerned if one of them were dropped than about the split.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture underlying superconducting quantum processors, flags his own closeness to that field, and worries about the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize.
responses.response: I take the scientific case seriously and agree it is a basic phenomenon turned into a platform. But I disagree that it should lead now. The 2025 prize is a close neighbour, so the committee would have to argue that strong coupling on a chip is a separate achievement. The theory credit (Blais, Huang, Girvin, Schoelkopf) is also split across more people than three names can cover, and Johansson himself says the allocation leaves out decisive contributors. I would keep B001 as a strong later candidate rather than this year's prize.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a new class of quantum matter classified by topology, and says the field is mature and arguably overdue, while noting the unresolved credit question around Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Moore.
responses.response: Topology as an organising principle is an idea I find compelling, and I would defend B019 as an alternative. My difficulty is the one Eriksson raises: the credited trio omits the HgTe proposal and the 3D work, so a defensible Kane-Mele-Molenkamp slate needs a citation narrow enough to stand against that history, and the 2016 prize already covers topological phases. I do not think the allocation is yet cleaner than that of the lattice clock, so I place it second, not first.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and the Event Horizon Telescope second, as detector-driven discoveries built on heavy calibration and background control, while admitting that credit in a large collaboration is contestable.
responses.response: I respect the measurement craft in both and agree the diffuse neutrino flux is secure. My reservations are about maturity and attribution. The origin of the flux is unresolved and point-source evidence is still at the few-sigma level, and for the EHT the shadow-size inference is modest as a gravity test and the roles are spread across hundreds of people. Pearce himself concedes both points. These are good second-tier cases, whereas the lattice clock is confirmed independently and the credit is easier to defend.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and how it would phrase the citation to show that.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto or others should displace or join Katori and Ye; I rely on recalled chronology.
Whether the KPZ case (B011) can be made with a clean credit line, given that Parisi and the authors of the exact solutions are not credited; I now judge this unlikely this year.
Timing relative to the pending SI redefinition of the second.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I share a Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers), but I have no known collaboration with any credited name; my KPZ ranking reflects my field of statistical physics, not a personal connection.
